newsitem.title: USA: Republicans, Democrats trade election charges.
newsitem.headline: Republicans, Democrats trade election charges.

text.p: With the race to control Congress heating up, Democrats and Republicans held duelling news conferences on Tuesday so each side could publicly claim it would trounce the other on Nov 5.

Republicans repeated their prediction that they would pick up 20-to-30 House of Representatives seats. Democrats, for their part, forecast a net gain of 30 seats -- well above the 19 needed to give them control of the 435-member House.

Independent analysts said they expected Republicans to keep control of the House and Senate, largely because Democrats must defend a big number of open seats in the South. But they added it was still too early to say.

"There are a number of factors that give the Republicans a slight edge in retaining the House and Senate. There are a lot of open seats in the South, and the likelihood of pickups there is not very great," said John Bibby, professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.
The Cook Political Report, which tracks congressional races, has also given Republicans a better-than-even chance of keeping the House.
PoliticsNow -- a partnership of ABC News, National Journal and The Washington Post -- issued an analysis on Friday saying Republicans would likely retain control of the Senate.

There are 53 open seats in the House, 30 of them due to Democratic retirements and 19 of those in the South where Republicans have come on strong in recent years. Democrats must also defend four open Senate seats in the South.
Texas Representative Martin Frost, chairman of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said Democrats would make major gains in the Northeast and possibly the West.

He also said losses would not be as great as expected in the South, pointing to Saturday's primary in Louisiana where it appeared two Democrats had won the right to face each other in a runoff for an open Republican House seat.
"We're going to pick up seats in every region of the country and fully expect to be in the majority after Nov. 5," Frost said.

Republicans drew a different message from Louisiana. Democrats had been expected to win the top two slots in a race for the open Senate seat of retiring Democrat Bennett Johnston, keeping Republicans out of a runoff.
Republicans at the last minute rallied around one candidate, Woody Jenkins, who came from behind to place first and face Democrat Mary Landrieu in November.
"The Democrats are in a state of disarray and panic," said Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, chairman of the Republican Senate Congressional Committee.
But both sides admit the outlook is much more competitive than was expected last year, when Republicans took control of both the House and Senate for the first time in 40 years.

Public approval of the Republican-led Congress dropped in the past 18 months as voters soured on their agenda. Democrats generally come out ahead in poll questions asking voters if they would prefer a Republican or Democratic House.

"There hasn't been a time in the past six months where the Republicans have actually taken the lead" in polls, said David Moore, managing editor of the Gallup Poll, calling the trend a generally positive sign for Democrats.

Democratic officials, who need to pick up four seats to control the Senate, say 17-20 Senate races are too close to call and are hoping President Clinton's double-digit lead in the polls will give them a boost.
Further, Democrats claim many of the 73 House freshmen Republicans are vulnerable and point to 14 Republican incumbents who they say trail their Democratic challengers.
Republicans point out that Democrats trail badly in some open Southern seats and have a list of vulnerable incumbents They also have millions of dollars more than Democrats.

National Congressional Committee Chairman Bill Paxon said he expected to retain every single Republican incumbent, hold nearly all open Republican seats and pick up nearly half of the 30 seats vacated by Democrats.
